articles.title: The second cup of coffee
articles.author: June Mercer
paragraphs: There is a familiar moment in every online evening. The coffee has cooled, the room is quiet, and a message from someone you have never met explains the very problem that occupied your afternoon. You write a reply. What began as a quick call becomes a conversation.

Online Weekly is for the time between those conversations. Each issue will contain something to try, something to argue with, and something worth saving for a disconnected afternoon. Our first rule is that a useful small example earns its space. Our second is that a reader should be able to tell an experiment from a promise.

Our imaginary December caller, Ellen, has a PC XT in the spare bedroom, a modem on the household telephone line, and a stack of unanswered questions about a printer. Before dialing, she writes three things on an index card: read the reply in the hardware forum, collect the recommended file description, and send the club secretary a short note. None requires buying another board. All require remembering why she called before an interesting conversation changes the plan. She gives herself a separate allowance for wandering through the service afterward.

That allowance matters because the clock is part of this kind of computing. Drafting a paragraph while connected consumes the same minutes as receiving useful information. Ellen prepares her question in a local editor, checks the spelling of the program name, and keeps the exact error message beside it. When the answer arrives, she captures it for reading after sign-off. This is not an argument against conversation. It is a way to reserve more of an evening's budget for the people and information that made the call worthwhile.

We also want room for owners whose machines seldom appear in the biggest advertisements. A C64 running a short program, an Apple II keeping a club list, and an ST beside a musical keyboard all belong at this table. Write to us about the job your computer actually does, including its irritating limitations. A letter about a disk that will not travel to a friend's machine may teach more than another argument about which processor deserves the future. Leave the coffee somewhere other than beside the diskette box, and tell us what happened.

This is a newly written fictional magazine inside the simulation. Our correspondents and their workshop anecdotes are invented. The questions, however, are familiar: what should I learn next, which part of my setup deserves attention, and how can I explain a problem clearly enough for somebody to help? Keep a notebook nearby. We intend to leave a few blank lines for your own answers.

articles.title: Two desks, two different bottlenecks
articles.author: Morgan Reed
paragraphs: Our imaginary test room contains two desks. At Desk A, an enthusiastic owner has a faster computer but a dim display, a cramped working surface, and one chair shared with the family. At Desk B, the machine is modest, the screen is comfortable to read, and the manuals are within reach. Which owner finishes a two-page club letter first?

There is no benchmark number in this comparison. We are comparing the whole task. Desk A spends ten minutes finding last month's address list. Desk B has the list filed with the previous letter. Desk A reformats a page after discovering that its printer settings differ from the document. Desk B has a note describing a working setup.

Give both desks the same fictional assignment: correct twelve addresses, merge them into a letter, and print a proof. Record separate times for opening the application, editing, preparing the merge, and printing. If the faster machine saves twenty seconds at startup but both owners spend ten minutes waiting for paper, the processor is not the immediate constraint. If a large worksheet takes minutes to recalculate after every change, the answer may be different. Separate the stages before deciding that a single total time explains the whole afternoon.

Storage deserves its own trial. A floppy-based owner may repeatedly exchange the program disk and the document disk. A hard disk can reduce that interruption, but it also introduces installation, backup, and compatibility questions. Extra RAM has a similar qualification: the application must be able to use the kind of memory being offered. An impressive total in an advertisement does not promise that an ordinary DOS program can load a larger document. Ask the demonstrator to run your actual job, with your intended version of the software and the necessary drivers installed.

Finally, perform the comparison in the room where the computer will live. Can you read a full page without reflections hiding the bottom lines? Is the printer reachable without stretching across a pile of disks? Does a second person need the desk for homework? Our worksheet has three columns headed delay, possible remedy, and proof. Put a movable lamp and a better filing arrangement on the same sheet as a faster system. The most useful purchase is the one that removes a measured difficulty without creating several expensive new ones.

A processor upgrade cannot supply those missing notes. Nor should a comfortable desk excuse hardware that cannot run the required application. Write down the job before comparing machines: the program, document size, printer, and time spent waiting. Then ask whether the delay comes from computation, the equipment around it, or the way the work is organized. The answer may be less glamorous than the advertisement and more useful on Monday morning.

articles.title: The three-line problem report
articles.author: BatchBeth
paragraphs: A good question does not have to fill a screen. Begin with three lines: what I tried, what I expected, and what happened. Add the computer and program version when they matter. The result is a starting point another member can actually use.

Compare "My printout is wrong" with "I printed a two-page letter using my saved settings. I expected the second page to start at the top margin. Instead it begins halfway down the sheet." The second report has not solved the problem, but it tells a helper what to examine. If you can repeat the result using a short sample document, mention that too.

Here is a report our fictional support desk can work with: 'IBM PC AT compatible, DOS 3.3, serial mouse and internal modem. I started the terminal program after loading the mouse driver. I expected both devices to work; the pointer stopped when the modem received data.' Add whether each device works alone and whether the failure began after a particular installation. Notice that the report does not announce a faulty motherboard. It separates observations from the owner's first theory, leaving room for another explanation.

A reply asking for the configuration is not a demand to upload every file on the disk. Copy the relevant lines from CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT, identify which driver belongs to which accessory, and omit personal details that have no bearing on the fault. Preserve the original configuration before an experiment. If an adviser suggests removing a driver, ask what function will be unavailable during the test and how to restore it. On a family computer, an unexplained change can turn one person's experiment into another person's missing printer or inaccessible application.

Close the exchange with a result that a stranger could reproduce. 'It works now' is cheerful but incomplete. Better: 'The two adapters shared an interrupt; the board manual listed another supported assignment. After that change, the mouse and modem worked together through a complete call.' Include anything still unresolved. If you cannot reproduce a suggestion, say so instead of silently treating it as disproved. Good forum troubleshooting resembles a shared laboratory notebook, even when the laboratory consists of one kitchen chair, a borrowed manual, and a very patient helper.

Do not change five settings while a reply is on its way. Keep the sample, record the starting conditions, and try one proposed change at a time. Report the result even when it does not help. The quiet follow-up saying "that did not change it" can save the next reader an evening. When the problem is solved, put the working result into the thread. A closed loop is more useful than a triumphant subject line with no explanation beneath it.

articles.title: Must every reply quote the whole message?
articles.author: The Mailbag
paragraphs: Dear Editor: I downloaded a discussion in which every reply included every previous reply. By the end, the original question occupied more space than the answers. Is there a polite way to ask for shorter quotations? -- A fictional reader signing as ShortLine

Our answer: quote the sentence you are answering, then add your response. Include a message number or a clear subject when the context would otherwise be lost. Brevity works best when it preserves the connection between question and answer. A reply consisting only of "yes" may be shorter and still force everybody to retrieve the old message.

Our mailbag also contains a practical objection: 'If I cut the quotation, won't the reply become meaningless in an offline capture?' It can, which is why a short identifying line earns its space. Include the forum, the earlier message number, and the part of the question being answered. Then quote a sentence if necessary. Someone paying to collect the discussion should not have to fetch six earlier messages just to discover whether your 'yes' concerns a cable, a software version, or the date of the next meeting.

Suppose a member writes three paragraphs about a modem and asks whether a replacement cable helped. A useful answer begins, 'Re your cable test in message 214: the shorter cable made no difference here.' Continue with the test conditions and result. Do not reproduce the unrelated paragraphs about the shop and the owner's holiday plans. Conversely, do not trim a sentence so aggressively that a cautious observation becomes a categorical claim. Quotation is a tool for accuracy. Saving characters at the cost of changing somebody's meaning is a poor bargain.

For club digests, put a brief editor's heading above a group of related replies and retain the original authors' handles. Ask before republishing private EasyPlex correspondence in a public discussion. A private answer may include details its author deliberately kept out of the forum. When permission is granted, state whether the text has been shortened. These small habits make a digest readable without pretending that the editor conducted every experiment. The best offline packet carries both the conclusion and enough of its route that another reader can question it intelligently.

Another reader, PaperTrail, asks whether a correction should replace an earlier claim. In a conversation, a follow-up explaining the correction is often clearer: identify the mistaken statement, supply the corrected information, and say what changed your mind. That gives later readers a usable trail. Nobody benefits from a discussion that appears to reach the right answer by magic. These letters are invented, but the invitation is real within the simulation: practice a concise reply in a forum thread.

articles.title: Make a useful capture, not a paper mountain
articles.author: June Mercer
paragraphs: For this weekend's project, choose one short discussion and turn it into a page you would want to reread. Save the text, give it a descriptive title, and add a note explaining the question it answered. Keep the original message numbers when available. Resist the temptation to capture every menu on the way there.

The difference between an archive and a heap is often the first sentence of the filename or heading. "Printer margin test, working result" will mean more next month than "session seven." If the discussion contains conflicting suggestions, leave a note distinguishing what was tried from what was merely proposed.

Try the assignment with a printer discussion. Capture the question, the relevant settings, and the final working result. In a separate note, record the machine, application version, printer mode, and date. The capture is your source; the note is your explanation of why you kept it. Retain an untouched original while removing menu repetitions from a working copy. Otherwise, a later edit can erase the one detail that explains why a promising suggestion failed. The extra copy is cheap compared with reconstructing a conversation from memory.

On a DOS disk, a name such as PRTMARG.TXT fits the familiar short filename convention. Put the longer description inside the file rather than trying to squeeze the whole story into eight characters. Start an INDEX.TXT with the filename, subject, source forum, and a sentence describing the result. Do not assume the extension alone identifies the contents: a captured listing, a formatted word-processing document, and an archive need different treatment. Open the file in the intended reader after saving it, particularly if you moved it between machines.

The final test takes place with the modem disconnected. Ask another club member to find the answer using only your index and packet. If they need to ask which message was decisive, add that information. If your printer splits a configuration line across two pages, revise the presentation without altering the command itself. A useful packet should survive both a screen and a modest printout. Keep the source date visible, because advice about a driver can become misleading after an upgrade. Then stop collecting for an evening and actually try the procedure you saved.

End with a question for your future self: what evidence would make this advice out of date? A different program version, a replacement interface, or a new printer could matter. A saved answer is most useful when its limits travel with it. Our challenge is one clear page, not the largest capture file. Leave some room for the next discovery.

articles.title: More RAM, same out-of-memory message
articles.author: DataDave
paragraphs: A member has bought additional memory for a PC compatible and still cannot open a larger worksheet. The dealer's receipt lists more RAM than the application reports. Is the board defective? Perhaps, but that is not the first conclusion to draw. On a DOS machine, the amount installed and the amount available to an ordinary application are different questions. Start by writing down the computer, DOS version, application version, expansion board, and driver. The answer depends on their combination, not on the largest number printed on the box.

Conventional memory is the familiar area below the PC's 640K boundary. DOS and resident software consume part of it before an application starts. Expanded memory, commonly discussed through the LIM specification, presents additional storage through a managed window; extended memory is a different arrangement above the first megabyte on suitable processors. They are not interchangeable labels. A program must support the relevant method to gain the intended benefit. Extra memory can therefore be present and useful for some purposes without making every existing program's main workspace larger.

Our fictional owner's worksheet manual lists expanded-memory support, while the proposed configuration offers extended memory without the required arrangement for that application. The corrective step is to consult the application and board documentation together, not to try random DEVICE lines from another member's setup. Ask which driver is required, which settings it expects, and how the program reports successful detection. A dealer demonstrating a different application has not yet demonstrated this one. Bring a representative worksheet with invented data so the test does not expose private business records.

Next examine the software already loaded. CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT may start device drivers and resident utilities that take memory needed by the application. List their purposes before removing anything. Make a known working boot copy and change one item at a time, keeping a written route back. A stripped-down setup that cannot access an essential device is not a practical solution merely because it reports a larger free-memory figure. Measure whether the real job works, then restore the features it actually requires.

Our comparison sheet records four observations: memory before loading the application, what the application detects, the largest representative job it handles, and any lost capability. It also records the exact configuration used. If the worksheet still fails, check whether its design or the program's own limits are responsible. Breaking a task into understandable parts may be more useful than installing a board that cannot address the bottleneck. Do not turn that possibility into a universal recommendation; some workloads really do benefit from supported expansion.

Bring the sheet to the hardware forum with the precise error text. Avoid a subject such as 'Memory is broken' when 'Worksheet cannot use newly installed expansion' describes the observation more accurately. Ask responders to name the application versions they have actually tried. This is an excellent example of why compatibility is a relationship among parts. A successful purchase ends with the intended worksheet opening, saving, and reopening correctly, and with a configuration note that lets its owner reproduce the result after the next round of experiments.

articles.title: Plan the call before the modem dials
articles.author: PacketPete
paragraphs: The least glamorous modem accessory is a short list of reasons for calling. Without one, a member can spend an evening looking for a file description, reading unrelated messages, and finally remembering the question that prompted the call. There is nothing wrong with an evening's conversation, but it should be a choice. Divide the plan into necessary work and browsing. Put the exact forum, subject, or filename beside each necessary item, and prepare any long outgoing text before connecting.

Our fictional budget uses an hourly service rate of twelve dollars only to illustrate the arithmetic. A fifteen-minute call at that rate costs three dollars before any other charges. Doubling the time doubles that part of the bill. A faster connection may shorten some transfers, but it does not shorten the minutes you spend thinking of a reply. Telephone charges, premium services, and rate periods can change the real total. Consult the actual applicable schedule rather than treating this worksheet or the simulator's figures as a historical tariff.

Make a call card with start time, intended tasks, an allowance for browsing, and a reminder to sign off. Read incoming messages into a capture when appropriate, then consider the answers offline. Draft a reply in plain text and inspect it before using the terminal's supported sending method. Avoid an improvised upload procedure that might insert editor control codes into a message. A test note is a better place to learn the process than an important letter addressed to a whole club.

Treat file transfers separately from ordinary reading. Note the file's size, intended machine, required companion files, and transfer method before starting. The terminal and remote service must agree on the transfer protocol. A directory listing that looks correct on screen does not guarantee a successful binary download. After receipt, inspect the accompanying documentation and verify the file through the tools appropriate to its format. Keep a record of the source and version so an interrupted or mistaken transfer can be discussed precisely.

A second card belongs beside the modem: the settings that work. Record the terminal program, data format, connection speed, and any initialization changes, with a copy of the unmodified setup. If the service looks garbled, investigate those facts before repeatedly changing everything. Distinguish failure to connect from a connection that produces unreadable text or one that drops after several minutes. Each observation narrows the question. A report containing the exact modem result and stage of failure gives another member a useful place to begin.

After sign-off, compare the plan with the call. Which tasks were completed, and which minutes bought nothing useful? Do the cost calculation with the actual assumptions written beside it. The goal is not to make every call joyless or mechanically brief. It is to stop avoidable searching and preparation from consuming the time you wanted for a good discussion. Save tomorrow's question while it is fresh, label the captured answers, and leave the terminal ready for another deliberate visit rather than another accidental marathon.

articles.title: A backup has to come back
articles.author: FloppyFran
paragraphs: A club member proudly brings a box labeled BACKUPS. Asked to recover last week's letter, he is uncertain which disk contains it and which program created the copies. The box may contain excellent protection, or merely a reassuring collection of plastic. A backup is a process with a return journey. Choose an ordinary test document and practice recovering it before trusting the arrangement with the only copy of a membership list, a manuscript, or several evenings of programming.

Begin by separating installation media, working data, and experiments. Keep the original program disks identified and use working copies where the software's instructions permit. Back up data often enough that losing the work since the last copy would be tolerable. A second file on the same physical disk may help with a mistaken edit, but it does not protect against loss of the disk itself. Use separate media for that purpose and keep a note explaining the date and contents of each set.

For a small floppy-based project, two alternating backup sets are easier to understand than a pile of unlabeled duplicates. Complete and check one before replacing the older useful copy. Do not assume that a copy operation succeeded merely because the drive stopped making noise. Read the saved document or compare the files using an appropriate utility. If your backup program creates its own archive format, keep the restoring program and instructions available. A collection that requires unavailable software cannot perform its intended rescue.

Practice recovery into a separate working location, never over the only current copy during the experiment. Give the recovered test file a distinguishable place or name and open it in its normal application. Does the formatting survive? Are the last changes present? Can a BASIC listing still be read to its final line? Write down the steps, including disk order if a set spans multiple diskettes. The practice should be simple enough that you can follow it when you are annoyed or tired.

Physical habits count too. Label disks clearly, handle them as their manufacturer instructs, and keep them away from spills and unsuitable storage conditions. Use media appropriate for the drive instead of assuming that a similar shape guarantees compatibility. If a disk repeatedly reports errors, preserve readable work before attempting experiments with repair utilities. A diagnostic test and a repair are different actions. Read what a utility changes before letting it act on a disk whose contents you cannot replace.

Our club's monthly backup exercise takes only one file. The owner supplies a copy and instructions; another member attempts the return journey. Missing labels and forgotten steps become obvious quickly. Add those discoveries to the procedure instead of depending on the original operator's memory. Once the process works for one representative item, extend it to the actual project. The reassuring box then earns its label: it contains not only copies, but an understood way of turning them back into useful work when the working disk is gone.

articles.title: Build a useful HyperCard stack on paper first
articles.author: MacMaven
paragraphs: HyperCard invites a Macintosh owner to organize an idea as a stack of cards, with fields for information and buttons for actions or movement. The invitation is wonderfully open-ended, which also makes it easy to begin decorating before deciding what the stack is for. Our fictional club chooses a modest project: an index of the books members may borrow. Before drawing a button, put five sample entries on actual index cards and ask a prospective borrower to find a particular title.

The paper exercise reveals the needed information: title, author, subject, owner, and whether the book is currently available. Some items belong on every card, while the contents change from book to book. HyperCard's backgrounds provide a way to share a design among cards. Keep the first design plain enough to expose errors in the information rather than conceal them. A well-drawn shelf is pleasant, but an accurately labeled title field does more for someone trying to borrow the programming manual before Saturday.

Give navigation a consistent pattern. A visitor should know how to reach the index and how to move through entries without hunting for a decorative object that secretly acts as a button. Make button labels describe the destination or action. Test the stack with one ordinary title, one very long title, a missing author, and two books with similar names. Those examples force decisions that a single perfect demonstration card avoids. Decide what an unknown value means instead of filling every empty field with a guess.

Our volunteer librarian discovers that availability changes more often than titles. She therefore needs a simple, reliable updating routine before adding clever searches. Use invented borrower details while demonstrating the design. Think about who may edit the real records and how a mistaken change would be recovered. Keep a separate backup before a major redesign. Information entered into a handsome stack is still information somebody must check, maintain, and restore. The computer does not make a borrowing policy or decide whether a book has actually been returned.

The first trial uses ten books and one helper who has not watched the author build the stack. Give the helper three tasks: find a book by subject, determine whether it is available, and return to the opening card. Observe where they hesitate without pointing at the screen. Revise the labels or arrangement when the hesitation reveals an assumption. Only then consider scripts that save repetitive work. A small understandable stack is a better foundation for learning HyperTalk than a large one whose basic navigation remains mysterious.

At the next meeting, bring both the stack and the paper plan. Explain one change that arose from testing, and identify the Macintosh setup used. Ask interested members what additional information would help, but resist adding every suggestion at once. A loan index that answers three common questions reliably already deserves to exist. Once it does that, you can explore new actions with a working example to compare against. The best introduction to an inviting tool is a modest problem whose successful solution can be recognized by somebody other than its author.

articles.title: One computer, three evenings of homework
articles.author: June Mercer
paragraphs: The family computer has acquired three owners without acquiring three keyboards. One person wants to finish a letter, another has a BASIC assignment, and a third has just discovered an adventure game. The argument is often presented as a hardware shortage, but the first useful upgrade may be a timetable and separate working disks. Our fictional household gives each project a place, a named file, and a clear stopping point. That makes it possible to leave the desk without relying on everybody else's memory.

Prepare a simple startup card for each regular task. Identify the program disk, data disk or directory, printer settings if needed, and the steps for saving. Do not let the family letter live under the same working filename as a school exercise simply because both authors accepted a program's default. On a DOS machine, a short personal directory can help; on a floppy-based system, distinct labels may be easier. Use the arrangement the household can maintain, not the most elaborate filing scheme an expert can devise.

Agree on what counts as an interruption. A player near a difficult section should know the scheduled finishing time before beginning. A writer should save before yielding the chair. A modem call may also occupy the household telephone line, so its reservation affects people beyond the desk. Put expected duration and a little cleanup time on the schedule. A plan that assumes nobody ever needs to finish a paragraph will fail; so will one that lets every game claim an unlimited final attempt.

For homework, the helper's job is to make the process understandable rather than produce the answer. Ask the learner to explain what a BASIC variable remembers, or to predict the effect of one change before running it. In a writing assignment, practice saving and reopening a short document before composing the whole essay. Printing a rough draft can reveal omissions that are harder to notice on a small screen. Keep the exercise appropriate to the learner, and do not mistake an attractive printout for evidence that the underlying work is understood.

Use invented names and numbers when teaching a database or spreadsheet. A child exploring commands should not be practicing on the only copy of a real address list. Keep the household's important data backed up separately, with a recovery method an adult has tried. Teach the difference between opening a document, changing it, and replacing the saved version. Those distinctions matter more than memorizing a long list of shortcuts. A family member who can recover from a harmless mistake has gained a practical skill, not merely permission to touch the machine.

End the week with a short review of what went wrong at the desk. Was a file hard to find, was the printer left in an unexpected mode, or did a call run through someone else's reservation? Fix one recurring difficulty. The computer need not become the center of every evening to be useful. A fair arrangement lets it serve different interests without turning one knowledgeable family member into a permanent operator. The best shared system is one people can start, use, save, and leave ready for the next person.

articles.title: A gift that gets used in January
articles.author: June Mercer
paragraphs: The holiday computer advertisement is a cheerful catalog of possibility. Every box promises a more capable desk. A useful gift begins with a less dramatic question: what does its recipient already enjoy doing?

The member who writes club letters may appreciate supplies for a known printer more than another unfamiliar program. A beginning programmer might prefer an afternoon of patient help with a tiny listing. A person who has carefully chosen a system may value a chance to select an accessory rather than an unexpected replacement for a part that already works.

For a diskette gift, copy the owner's requirements exactly: physical size, density, and intended drive. Two disks that fit through similar openings need not be suitable substitutes. Ask which boxes the owner already buys instead of guessing that a more expensive density must be better. For a printer ribbon, take the full printer model to the shop. A nearly correct cartridge is still an unusable cartridge, and the recipient should not have to spend the holiday tracing the source of a well-meant purchase.

Software needs an equally specific card. Write down the computer family, operating system, available memory, disk drives, and display. If the program expects a mouse, hard disk, or particular graphics adapter, include that cost in the gift. Ask what the package actually contains: program disks, a manual, registration material, and any required accessories. A friend may enjoy a new adventure game but have no interest in a complex spreadsheet. The right category depends on the recipient's evenings, not on which demonstration drew the largest crowd in the shop.

Our most successful fictional gift is a Saturday afternoon reserved for a project. One member offers to help another prepare a newsletter master, make a backup, and print enough copies for the January meeting. The owner chooses the software and keeps the finished files. Nobody promises that the computer will become effortless. Instead, the gift removes a specific obstacle and leaves a repeatable process. Put a written description of that promise in an envelope if a box seems necessary. A useful afternoon can outlast the appeal of another accessory that has no assigned job.

Our fictional gift desk has no sales counter. We are offering a method: ask about the task, confirm compatibility, and leave the recipient a choice when the answer is uncertain. Manuals, labels, and the time to organize a project rarely appear in the most exciting photographs. They can nevertheless be the gifts still in use after the wrapping paper has disappeared. This week we compare working habits, consider a club exchange, and ask readers what made an earlier gift memorable.

articles.title: A printer comparison without a winner
articles.author: Morgan Reed
paragraphs: Imagine two club members comparing printers. One needs inexpensive draft copies and does not mind a noisy afternoon. The other prepares finished letters in a shared room and cares about appearance and disturbance. A review that announces one universal winner has already discarded half the problem.

Bring a sample of your own work to a demonstration. A page of large display lettering is not the same test as a letter with small text, a table, and a second page. Ask to see the entire process: opening the document, choosing settings, producing the page, and dealing with a simple correction. Note the application and settings so the result can be reproduced.

Our comparison sheet begins with three jobs: a rough draft, a finished letter, and a page containing a small table. A dot-matrix printer may be attractive for routine drafts and continuous stationery; a daisy-wheel machine may appeal to someone chiefly concerned with letter text; a laser printer invites more ambitious page design. Those descriptions do not settle the purchase. Ask about the actual model's capabilities, supplies, paper handling, and application support. A beautiful sample produced by unfamiliar software tells you little about the results from your own word processor.

Time the complete page rather than the first burst of movement. Include time spent preparing the document and feeding the next sheet. Listen from the adjacent room. If you use multipart forms, bring a sample and ask whether that printer is intended to handle them; do not infer suitability from a general speed claim. For envelopes, verify the supported size and feeding procedure. Check where continuous paper will rest before and after printing. A compact printer can require a surprisingly large working area once the paper path is included.

Make the last trial a deliberately ordinary correction: change one address and print the page again. Can the owner restore the settings without the dealer's help? Does the cable supplied match the computer's interface, and is the correct driver available for the application version? Record the answers alongside consumable costs and the quoted package contents. We would choose different machines for different desks. That is the point of the exercise. A purchase becomes easier to defend when the comparison sheet describes your work instead of borrowing the priorities of an advertisement.

Supplies and connections deserve a line on the comparison sheet alongside the purchase itself. So do space and the people who share it. We are not assigning scores to historical models or claiming measurements from a real bench. The comparison is an exercise in choosing the right questions. Decide what a satisfactory page looks like before admiring the fastest demonstration.

articles.title: The exchange table needs an index
articles.author: DiskDaisy
paragraphs: Our fictional club exchange began with a generous pile of disks and an immediate shortage of explanations. One label said "utilities." Another said "new." A third named a person who had already gone home. The first volunteer spent the evening asking what each disk contained.

For the next meeting, every contribution gets a card: title, version, intended machine, contents, and the contributor's handle. It also says whether the material may be copied. A useful description is more than a list of exciting nouns. "Plain-text worksheet; no program to install" tells a newcomer something that "productivity package" does not.

The next exchange table has three clearly marked areas: readable documents, programs to evaluate, and commercial-package demonstrations that are not being distributed. A volunteer records the author's copying instructions with each item rather than assuming that anything on a club disk is free for every purpose. Shareware is especially easy to misunderstand. Distribution permission and continued-use terms are separate questions. Keep the registration notice and documentation with the program. A collection stripped of those files is less useful to the next member and unfair to the person who wrote it.

Give each disk an inventory that can be read before running anything. Our sample entry reads, 'CALLCOST.BAS, GW-BASIC text listing, estimates a fictional connect charge; enter minutes and an hourly rate; no account connection.' That tells the reader what to expect and what not to expect. Add the version and the name of the person who checked the copy. A label saying 'tested' is incomplete unless it says on which machine and with which interpreter. A successful demonstration on a PC does not establish that an Apple II can load the same disk.

The club secretary keeps a correction sheet beside the index. If a member discovers a missing final line, a mislabeled version, or a program that needs an additional file, the correction travels with later copies. New arrivals go through the same process instead of quietly replacing a known working disk. Nobody needs a grand bureaucracy; a numbered card and a legible note will do. At closing time, the table should contain identifiable contributions whose origins and instructions remain attached. Generosity becomes more valuable when the recipient can tell exactly what was given.

The index should identify a small, understandable starting point. New members do not need to leave with every file on the table. They need one item they can open, try, and discuss. Keep the cards with the contributions and note any corrected versions. A good exchange ends with fewer mysteries than it began with. The most appreciated contribution may be the careful index itself.

articles.title: The unwanted upgrade
articles.author: The Mailbag
paragraphs: Dear Editor: My family knows I like computers and wants to buy an upgrade. I am pleased, but I have just made my present setup reliable. How can I explain that another project is not the same as a present? -- Fictional correspondent QuietBoot

We suggest describing something you would enjoy doing with the gift. "I would like supplies for the newsletter" is easier to act on than a list of reasons every proposed accessory is wrong. If the family wants a surprise, offer several compatible possibilities. A promise to choose an item together can still be a thoughtful present.

QuietBoot's follow-up makes the problem more concrete: the proposed present is extra memory, but the intended spreadsheet may need a particular expansion arrangement. The family has sensibly asked before buying. We would take the application manual and the machine details to the dealer together, then request a demonstration of the actual benefit. Capacity by itself is not enough information. A board that physically fits can still require drivers, settings, or software support that the current owner does not have. Nobody should feel ungrateful for asking those questions first.

For a less technical wish list, specify useful quantities and models: a compatible ribbon, the right diskettes, a binder that holds the program manuals, or a reference book pitched at the reader's experience. Include one project you would like to attempt with company. Our fictional reader RibbonRoad adds that an offer to type old club membership cards into a database was a better present than an unfamiliar application. The work included checking the entries afterward, which made it a gift of attention rather than merely a pile of newly typed errors.

A final reader asks whether to sell an old accessory immediately to make room for its replacement. We would first establish that the new arrangement performs the familiar job and that a useful backup exists. Pack the older device with its cable, manual, and settings sheet if it is going to another owner. An upgrade is most pleasant when it has an orderly beginning and end. Agreeing on a trial and keeping the receipt need not spoil the surprise. It simply leaves the recipient able to enjoy the present without inheriting a mystery.

Reader RibbonRoad remembers a more modest success: a friend labeled a stack of workshop notes and made a readable index. The gift was time, not a machine, and it made the existing equipment more useful. Both letters remind us that the owner's interests come before a product category. The fictional names belong to this magazine; the exercise is to write a short wish list based on tasks rather than advertising slogans.
related: GO NOTEBOOK - draft a task-based wish list

articles.title: One page, one experiment
articles.author: BatchBeth
paragraphs: Choose a task you repeat and prepare a one-page experiment. At the top, write the starting conditions. In the middle, leave room for one change and its result. At the bottom, reserve a line for the next person who will try it.

An example might compare two ways of organizing a newsletter's working files. Use the same small project in each trial. Time spent locating the correct file counts; so does time spent recovering from an ambiguous name. Do not turn a comparison of filing methods into a simultaneous test of a new editor and a new printer.

For a more technical example, compare two printer modes using the same half-page letter. Put a date, a few numbers, and a short table in the sample. Record which mode was selected in the application and on the printer. Time from the print command until the page is ready to remove, then inspect the result at normal reading distance. A fast draft and a slower finished copy may both be useful. The experiment should discover when you would choose each, not force one mode to win every possible job.

Include a place for surprises. Perhaps the second mode changes line breaks, or the table no longer fits within the margins. That is a result, not an inconvenience to hide. Restore the first settings and repeat the original sample to check that the difference follows the change. If it does not, look for another variable: different paper, a changed document, or an application option left over from an earlier job. A single successful printout is encouraging, but a repeatable comparison provides a firmer basis for changing your regular setup.

Bring the sheet and both printouts to the club. Another member can try the same document on a different machine while keeping your conditions visible. The second result may show that your conclusion applies only to one driver or printer combination. Write that limit down. Over several meetings, a small collection of such reports can become a useful local buying and troubleshooting reference. It will be less glamorous than a table of unexplained scores, but much easier to trust when somebody asks what will happen to their own two-page letter.

When you finish, explain the result in ordinary language. "The second arrangement kept originals separate from working copies" is more useful than declaring it a breakthrough. File the page with the project and bring it to the next club meeting. The experiment is small enough to repeat and concrete enough to argue about. That combination is the beginning of a useful workshop conversation.
related: GO COMMODORE - application-test worksheets and discussions

articles.title: The 286, the 386, and the job on your desk
articles.author: VGAVal
paragraphs: A December computer advertisement can make an existing PC feel obsolete before its owner has finished the morning's letter. Faster processors, larger disks, and impressive memory figures invite a simple ranking. Yet a PC XT, an AT-class compatible, and a 386 system do not become sensible choices in that order for every household. Begin with the software you intend to use and the work that currently makes you wait. A system that wins a demonstration of somebody else's task may be an expensive answer to a question you never asked.

For our fictional club buyer, the work is a word-processing document, a membership database, and a moderately large spreadsheet. Prepare representative copies and ask the dealer to open, edit, calculate, save, and print them. Time each stage separately. Processor speed can matter during calculation while disk access dominates loading. Printer speed may dominate the final report. A stopwatch beside a real task gives the discussion firmer ground than a single synthetic score. Record the configuration as well as the time, because a demonstration machine may contain options absent from the quoted package.

Check memory in terms the application understands. A large installed total does not automatically become conventional workspace for a DOS program. Ask what type of expansion is supplied and whether the intended version of the software uses it. The 386's capabilities are interesting, but software must take advantage of them to deliver a particular benefit. Do not pay for an unexplained promise that every old program will become dramatically different. Ask the demonstrator to identify which part of your test benefits and by how much.

Compatibility deserves an entire page of notes. List the expansion boards, display, printer, modem, and diskettes you hope to carry forward. A physically similar slot or connector is not a sufficient guarantee. Check the computer and accessory documentation together. Try old working media in the intended drives, using copies rather than irreplaceable originals. Include software installation and printer configuration in the exercise. An upgrade that runs the spreadsheet faster but cannot conveniently exchange the club's disks has introduced a cost that belongs in the decision.

Compare complete quotations: system unit, display, storage, memory, interfaces, operating system, manuals, and any installation service. Ask who handles a fault and what equipment must be returned. This article supplies no invented market prices or universal winner. The club can make its own table from actual offers available to its members. Keep those offers dated and distinguish a cash price from a package containing extra equipment. An apparently cheaper machine may simply omit the component that makes the demonstration useful.

Our buyer leaves with a test sheet rather than an order. The existing machine remains adequate for letters, but the representative worksheet establishes a real reason to investigate a faster system. That is progress. The next visit can compare two complete configurations against an explicit acceptance test. Sometimes the right answer will be to buy; sometimes it will be to improve storage, revise the task, or wait. The computer worth owning is the one whose capabilities meet your work at a cost you can explain.
related: GO IBMHW - discuss a complete configuration
GO SHOP - inspect the fictional catalog

articles.title: CGA, EGA, VGA: look beyond the color count
articles.author: EGAEd
paragraphs: The display is the part of a computer an owner looks at for the whole evening, yet it is often chosen from a few minutes of colorful demonstration. A game picture and a page of small text ask different things of a screen. Before comparing adapters, decide which programs matter and which modes they use. A writer may care more about legible characters than a richer picture, while a drawing enthusiast may put another capability first. Neither should have to borrow the priorities of the shop's demonstration disk.

CGA, EGA, and VGA describe different display standards, not a promise that every monitor can accept every signal. Check the exact adapter and monitor combination in their documentation. Do not experiment by attaching a convenient-looking plug to an unsuitable display. Some systems and monitors support more than one mode, but that support must be established for the actual equipment. A label on the front of a game box also deserves reading: determine which graphics modes its version offers before assuming a new board changes the picture.

Bring a page of the text you normally read and a representative application. Examine the full screen, including its corners. Can you distinguish punctuation, similar letters, and the selected item? Try the colors or intensity settings you expect to use at home. Look at the display from the chair position and room lighting you can reasonably reproduce. A picture that looks spectacular in a dark corner of the shop may be tiring in a bright spare bedroom. The whole working environment belongs in the comparison.

For games, ask to see the exact machine version rather than a screenshot from another system. Check whether older favorites offer a compatible mode and whether any board-specific setting is required. Keep a written record of changes so ordinary word-processing work can be restored afterward. Do not assume that an unfamiliar scrolling problem proves the monitor is failing. It may require investigation of the software and display combination. Describe the affected program, mode, and adapter when asking the forum; 'bad picture' leaves too many possibilities open.

Our fictional club conducts a useful blind comparison by hiding the price cards and showing a letter, a table, and a game scene on each complete setup. Members record what is readable and what matters to them before discussing specifications. Then the cards return, along with the equipment requirements and included cables. The exercise does not turn personal preference into a laboratory measurement. It makes preference explicit and prevents an impressive color count from silently deciding a purchase whose main purpose is writing several pages every night.

Keep the final test ordinary. Open the familiar program, perform a short task, and restore the usual mode without assistance. If several people share the machine, let each try it. A display upgrade succeeds when it improves the work or recreation the household actually does. Record the supported combination and useful settings with the system notes. The next time a game or application looks wrong, those notes provide a known starting point instead of another evening of guessing which switch was moved during the last demonstration.
related: GO FORUMS - Gamers Forum: compare machine versions

articles.title: Mail merge without fifty embarrassing letters
articles.author: WordPro
paragraphs: Mail merge promises a small miracle: one carefully written letter becomes a personalized copy for every club member. It also offers an efficient way to repeat one mistake fifty times. Before loading expensive stationery, create a trial list of invented people and a short letter containing every field you intend to use. The exact commands differ among word processors, so keep the program's merge instructions nearby. The first exercise should establish that the data, field names, and printed layout agree before the real mailing enters the process.

Choose sample records that expose awkward cases. Include a long surname, an apartment line, an organization instead of a personal name, and a missing optional field. Decide how the greeting should read in each case. A blank field can leave an unwanted line or an absurd salutation if the template assumes every record has the same shape. Do not correct only the printed copy. Fix the template or the data so the same defect cannot recur when the list is used again next month.

Inspect the address list as data, not merely as a page that looks tidy. If the program expects a particular delimiter or field order, preserve it. A comma inside a name or address can matter when exchanging records through a comma-delimited format; use the application's documented import rules. Keep the original list before conversion. Count records before and after importing, and check the first, last, and deliberately awkward samples. A successful import message does not establish that every address landed in the intended field.

Print the trial on ordinary paper and examine the entire page. Check where a long address wraps, where the date appears, and whether the second page begins sensibly. If you plan to print envelopes or labels, make a separate alignment test using suitable plain paper before committing the final supplies. Printer modes and application settings should be recorded with the template. A margin that worked for a normal letter may not suit a different form, and an attractive screen preview cannot account for every paper-feeding problem.

Our fictional secretary asks another member to proofread the trial without showing them the underlying data. Can they identify the recipient and understand the greeting? Then compare the printout with the records. This catches errors a person who has stared at the template all afternoon may overlook. For a real club list, limit copies to people who need them and use invented data at public demonstrations. Convenience in producing correspondence is not a reason to distribute everyone's address along with the example template.

Once the test passes, save the template, the checked data, and a brief settings note under identifiable names. Print a small initial batch from the real list and inspect it before the whole run. Keep a count of produced copies so an interruption does not lead to duplicate mailings. The reward is not only fifty letters. It is a repeatable routine in which the next secretary can change the message, verify a few samples, and understand exactly which information is being merged into each finished page.
related: GO NOTEBOOK - save the merge checklist

articles.title: Shareware: keep the author's instructions in the package
articles.author: SharewareSam
paragraphs: A useful utility arrives from a forum library, performs its advertised job, and asks the reader to register. One club member calls it free software because no shop took payment before the download. Another assumes every program passed around on disk has the same terms. Both assumptions skip the most useful file in the package: the author's explanation. Shareware describes an approach to distribution and evaluation, but the actual instructions govern the particular program. Read them before deciding what to keep using or what to pass along.

Make the first inspection an inventory. Locate the program, documentation, version identification, registration information, and any examples. Determine the intended machine and required operating environment. An archive is a container, not an application to be executed simply because it arrived successfully. Use a suitable extraction tool and keep the original archive while evaluating its contents. If a required file appears missing, compare the inventory with the documentation before assuming that an error message means the software itself is defective.

Evaluate with a disposable example rather than the only copy of important work. A disk utility deserves particular attention to what it reads and what it changes. A text formatter can be tried on a short invented document. A catalog program can index a small test directory. Record the input, expected result, and actual result. The point is to learn whether the utility fits your job, including the awkward parts, before allowing a successful demonstration to become an unexamined place in the regular workflow.

If you choose to register, follow the author's stated procedure and retain the relevant details with your software records. Distinguish a registration payment from a donation and from a charge made by a disk distributor for supplying media. They need not serve the same purpose. If the instructions are unclear or absent, seek clarification instead of inventing permission. Our simulation's shareware service is fictional; it provides a place to explore these habits, not an order channel for the historical authors whose programs members may remember.

When sharing a permitted copy, keep notices and documentation attached and identify whether you have modified anything. A friend who receives only an executable loses the instructions needed to use it and understand its terms. Avoid relabeling a personal patch as the author's next version. If you report a defect, include a small reproducible example, the original version number, and your environment. An accurate report offers more help than a declaration that the program failed somewhere during an evening of unrelated experiments.

Our club software shelf keeps one card per evaluated package: what it does, how it was tested, where it came from, what is required, and where its distribution instructions are found. The card does not replace the author's documentation. It helps the next member decide whether the package is relevant before spending time obtaining it. A healthy exchange depends on both curiosity and care: curiosity to try a useful idea, and care to preserve the context that lets its author and its next user remain part of the conversation.
related: GO SHAREWARE - explore fictional registration and support
GO DOSLIB - inspect documented program listings

articles.title: Buying a game for the machine you actually own
articles.author: ByteBender
paragraphs: The holiday game shelf is a contest of promises. A painted cover suggests an immense world, while a tiny requirements panel decides whether that world can appear on your desk. Read the small panel first. Identify the exact computer version, disk format, memory needs, input devices, and display requirements. A familiar title on a different system may have different graphics, sound, controls, or loading behavior. A shop demonstration or a friend's enthusiastic report is most useful when it refers to the version you can actually run.

Ask what kind of evening the game wants. A short action game may suit ten minutes before supper; a large adventure or role-playing game may reward notes, saved progress, and longer sessions. Wasteland is among the titles occupying adventure discussions this year, but the existence of an absorbing long game does not mean every recipient wants that commitment. A gift should match the player's interests as well as the computer. Find out whether they enjoy exploration, puzzles, competition, or building an understanding of rules over repeated attempts.

For a boxed adventure, examine the included material. Manuals, maps, reference cards, and other supplied items can be part of the intended experience. A used copy missing its instructions may be less of a bargain than its price suggests. Ask how progress is saved and what working media are needed, following the game's documentation. Keep the original disks handled and stored appropriately. Do not assume that every game uses the same copying or saving procedure simply because two packages arrive on the same size diskette.

For action games, try the intended keyboard, joystick, or mouse arrangement if the dealer offers a demonstration. A control scheme that feels comfortable to one player may be frustrating to another. Ask whether difficulty or sound can be adjusted for the household. Listen at a realistic volume and look at the display the buyer will use. A photograph or another machine's impressive sound system can set expectations the actual version does not promise. Write down what was demonstrated so memories of several packages do not merge into one impossible ideal.

A good forum review separates description from judgment. Explain the version, setup, opening experience, and what sort of play holds your interest. Identify whether you reached a conclusion or only tried the first portion. Keep solutions out of subject lines and mark detailed hints clearly. Another member should be able to decide whether the game appeals without accidentally receiving the answer to its central puzzle. Price and performance comparisons also need dates and equivalent configurations rather than a mixture of remembered offers.

Our fictional club's best gift recommendation is sometimes a joint visit to the shop and an evening set aside to learn the controls. That gives the recipient a choice and a companion without forcing a purchase based only on a cover. Once a game has been chosen, include the patient first session: read the instructions, establish the saving routine, and let the player explore. The computer version is the entry ticket. The right match between the game and the person is what makes the ticket worth keeping.
related: GO FORUMS - Gamers Forum: exchange reviews and spoiler-marked hints
GO GAMES - try the simulator's games

articles.title: The pleasure of finishing something
articles.author: June Mercer
paragraphs: The new computer libraries give this week's issue a useful theme: programs small enough to finish reading. A docking game, an arithmetic exercise, a timing calculator, and a one-room adventure make modest promises. You can inspect the numbered lines instead of taking the description on faith.

That is a different pleasure from opening a large commercial package. The small listing invites questions. Why does this branch run? What does that variable remember? What happens if the player asks for something impossible? A beginner can change a message and see the result without understanding every corner of the machine.

A small program also makes ownership feel different. When a menu prints the wrong instruction, you can find the PRINT statement and correct it. When an answer seems odd, follow the calculation with pencil and paper. Begin with an original copy stored separately from the experiment. Write the interpreter and intended machine at the top of the listing, because similar BASIC names conceal real differences. Even a program that uses only numbers and text can encounter different file-loading conventions or error behavior on another computer.

Set a finish line before adding features. For the call-cost calculator, the first finish line might be three known calculations and a clear description of excluded charges. Printing a decorative heading can wait until those results are right. For an adventure, it might be one puzzle with a successful path and sensible responses to premature actions. A beginner who completes that much has already met variables, decisions, and the difference between an imagined rule and a rule the machine actually follows. Those are substantial accomplishments even when the screen contains no animation.

Our club's fictional review evening gives every author five minutes to demonstrate a program and five minutes to watch another person use it. The second half is usually more revealing. An unfamiliar user presses RETURN at an unexpected moment, enters a fraction at a menu, or assumes that SAVE means saving a game rather than leaving an editor. Write down those moments. Choose one to improve and leave the rest for another version. A finished small program is not a flawless program; it is a comprehensible promise with a result someone else can reproduce.

Our reviews concern original programs supplied with this simulation. They are not claims about recovered 1988 software. The workshop spirit is the part we want to preserve: try a known example, keep the original, and explain one change to somebody else. Finishing a small project does not mean running out of ambition. It means having a result solid enough to build on next week.
related: GO C64LIB - Commodore and Amiga collection

articles.title: DOCK64: gravity reads the instructions
articles.author: SectorSam
paragraphs: DOCK64.BAS offers a landing pad, a fuel allowance, and a remarkably unsympathetic gravity calculation. Choose thrust from zero through five each turn. The display reports altitude, downward speed, and remaining fuel. A gentle landing requires a speed of two or less when the craft reaches the pad.

The useful lesson arrives when a player spends fuel merely postponing the fall. You need a plan for the final descent, not an impressive moment of hovering. The companion C64NOTES.TXT provides a reproducible safe flight, so a newcomer can first verify the listing and then experiment. Follow that flight exactly and the current version should finish with three fuel units.

Before attempting a personal record, copy a four-column log onto paper: turn, altitude, downward speed, and fuel. Add the thrust choice beside each row. This exposes the difference between slowing a descent and merely choosing a large number because the ground looks close. Compare two runs that differ in only one early choice. If you change every decision, you may get a better result without understanding why. The simple display is an advantage here: the information needed to explain a landing is visible instead of buried behind a picture of a spacecraft.

A useful club challenge is to explain a failed flight without changing the listing. Did the pilot spend too much fuel early, wait too long to brake, or misunderstand the speed sign? Let one person make choices while another records the numbers. Switch roles for the next run. Keep the companion notes nearby to distinguish a typing error from a poor plan. If the documented check flight behaves differently, inspect the entered lines before inventing a new theory about the game's physics. A missing minus sign can look remarkably like a difficult simulation.

Only after those checks would we alter the program. Change a displayed message first, then perhaps an initial allowance, and repeat a recorded flight to see what differs. Preserve the original under its supplied name and label the experiment clearly. This is a classroom-scale numerical toy, not a model for operating real vehicles. Its value lies in making cause and effect discussable. A successful evening ends with a pilot who can explain why a particular decision helped, a legible flight log, and enough curiosity to try another controlled experiment next time.

We like the visible numbers and the absence of hidden controls. We would not recommend it to someone seeking elaborate graphics or a long campaign. Its replay value comes from understanding a simple model and improving a sequence of choices. The download is an ASCII BASIC listing, not a C64 disk image. Read its type-in instructions before attempting to load it as a native program. Then keep a flight log and see whether your second plan is better than your first.

articles.title: An adventure with three things to remember
articles.author: BatchBeth
paragraphs: LOSTDISK.BAS needs only a few pieces of state: the player's choice, whether a key has been found, and whether the missing disk has been collected. Its room description is small because the exercise is about how those facts change the available result.

Begin by trying the cabinet before the desk. It should remain locked. Try returning the disk before taking it; the program should refuse. Then inspect the desk, revisit the cabinet, and return the recovered disk. These are different paths through the same short listing. Testing only the successful path would miss half the point.

Draw a table with three rows before adding that object. The first row describes the room before finding the key, the second describes the unlocked cabinet, and the third describes possession of the disk. Beside each state, list the actions that should succeed and the messages for actions that should fail. This is a compact design document. It helps prevent the familiar beginner's mistake of adding an exciting command that works regardless of whether the player has earned it. The story and the variables should describe the same situation.

Now choose an extension that introduces only one new fact. A note in the desk might explain which cabinet contains the disk, while a LOOK NOTE action repeats the explanation after discovery. Decide whether reading is required or merely helpful. Those choices lead to different tests: attempting the cabinet without reading, reading twice, and returning to the note after finishing. Do not add a second room, inventory weight, and a timer during the same experiment. Each may be interesting, but together they make it harder to identify the source of a wrong response.

Ask a partner to explore with no verbal coaching. Keep a copy of the exact commands they try, including reasonable words the program does not recognize. A short adventure can acknowledge a synonym or print the available choices without becoming a full language parser. If you keep a numbered menu, make its numbers consistent after the new action is added. Finish by restoring the original successful sequence and confirming it still reaches the ending. The extension has earned its place when it creates an understandable choice rather than merely increasing the listing's length.

For a club extension, design one additional object on paper before editing any code. Write down where it is found, which variable remembers it, and what action it enables. Also decide what the program says when that action is attempted too early. Keep the original listing and give your altered version a different name. A larger room is not automatically a better adventure. A clear cause and effect is the improvement worth demonstrating.

articles.title: Why will this BAS file not load?
articles.author: The Mailbag
paragraphs: Dear Editor: I downloaded a listing and expected a ready-to-run disk file. The instructions say to enter the numbered lines. Have I received the wrong file? -- Fictional correspondent LoadAgain

Not necessarily. The BASIC files in the new community collection are readable text. A native saved program may contain tokens or other structure that a plain listing does not contain. The filename extension alone cannot promise the machine's preferred on-disk representation. Use the instructions for the indicated interpreter and preserve work already in memory before replacing it.

The transfer itself is another layer. Reading a program on screen and saving a terminal capture can introduce headings, prompts, or wrapped lines that do not belong in the listing. Use the library's file download procedure when available, then inspect the saved text. Check the opening line, the final line, quotation marks, and any long statement that might have been split. A readable filename is not proof that the file arrived intact. Preserve the downloaded original and perform repairs in a second copy so you can compare them later.

The destination interpreter must also understand the statements. A program that calls a machine-specific graphics routine cannot be made portable simply by renaming its file. Even ordinary examples should identify the dialect and avoid implying that identical-looking LOAD commands have identical behavior. If you type the numbered lines manually, LIST the program afterward and compare it with the source in short sections. Check punctuation before assuming a complex fault. Letter O and digit zero, or a missing quotation mark, can cause an error far removed from the line you intended to enter.

Our ideal problem report therefore has three parts: where the file came from, how it reached the computer, and what the interpreter did with it. Include the program version and the first exact error. If you used a present-day emulator to explore this historical collection, identify that separately from the intended original machine. The editorial examples are designed to evoke a 1988 type-in evening, but the delivery routes available to today's reader are broader. Good instructions make that distinction explicit instead of blaming the owner for expecting a different kind of file.

GW-BASIC can load the supplied DOS ASCII listings directly. For the other intended systems, the collection describes entering the lines or using an emulator's supported text-paste facility. It does not supply disk images. Our checks exercised the shared BASIC logic in PC-BASIC, not every original machine's import process. That distinction belongs in a review as well as a file description. If you report a problem, say how you entered the program and include the exact message, not just "the download failed."

articles.title: A calculator needs an answer sheet
articles.author: ClockworkST
paragraphs: TEMPO.BAS and CALLCOST.BAS solve different little problems, but they share a useful testing method: start with an input whose answer you already know. At 120 beats per minute, the tempo calculator should report 500 milliseconds for a quarter note and two seconds for a four-beat bar. Thirty minutes at a fictional twelve-dollar hourly rate should produce six dollars in the session calculator.

Next try a boundary or an invalid input. Does the program reject it, finish, or accept it deliberately? Read the opening instructions before deciding that a result is a defect. TEMPO assumes four quarter-note beats per bar; it is not discovering a song's time signature. CALLCOST omits surcharges and does not change your account.

Build a small answer sheet for CALLCOST with minutes in one column, the assumed hourly rate in another, and the expected charge in a third. Fifteen minutes at twelve dollars an hour is three dollars; five minutes at six dollars an hour is fifty cents. These are illustrative rates, not a published tariff. Include zero minutes as a boundary to examine against the program's stated input rules. A rejection can be correct if the instructions require a positive session length. What matters is agreement between the promise and the behavior.

For TEMPO, double the beats per minute and predict the effect before running it. The interval between quarter notes should halve. Under its four-beat-bar assumption, sixty beats per minute means one second per quarter note and four seconds per bar. A musician using another meter must not mistake that final number for a universal measure. Write the assumption next to the result, especially if copying it into a delay or practice worksheet. Units are part of the answer: a bare 500 can mean something very different from 500 milliseconds.

Now give a partner the answer sheet without your preferred sequence of inputs. Ask them to choose a case, predict the result, and explain any disagreement. This catches misunderstandings that repeated runs of the same demonstration can conceal. If you revise an input check or a displayed label, run the old cases again and add one that exercises the change. Keep the sheet with the listing. A few known answers make a small BASIC utility easier to improve, easier to teach, and much harder to trust merely because it produces a plausible-looking number.

Write three expected results beside the listing before making an alteration. Run them again afterward. The answer sheet need not be elaborate to be useful. It is a promise you can check, and it turns a vague feeling that the program still works into a small piece of evidence.

articles.title: Find the first wrong number
articles.author: BASICBob
paragraphs: A short BASIC program prints a plausible total that is nevertheless wrong. Its author reads the listing from top to bottom three times, then changes a line that looks suspicious. The new answer is different, which feels like progress, but nobody knows whether it is better. Start instead with the smallest input whose answer you can calculate by hand. Write the expected intermediate values beside the listing. The useful question is not 'Where does this program look odd?' It is 'Where does the actual calculation first disagree with the expected one?'

Our example converts minutes and an hourly charge into a session estimate. With fifteen minutes and a rate of twelve dollars per hour, the calculation should produce three dollars. The expression minutes divided by sixty, multiplied by the rate, makes the units visible. A mistaken division by the rate produces a different operation even if one special test happens to look reasonable. Try a second case with a different rate. A test that changes only the minutes may conceal an error tied to the rate itself.

Add temporary PRINT statements after input and after each important calculation. Label their output so a column of numbers does not become another mystery. Verify that the variables hold what you intended before testing a later branch. If the first value is wrong, investigate input or assignment rather than adjusting the final formula to compensate. Keep a clean copy of the program before adding tracing statements. Once the fault is understood, remove the temporary output and repeat the same cases on the version you intend to distribute.

For loops, choose a tiny range and count the expected passes on paper. A loop intended to process three entries should not silently process four because the author counted both endpoints incorrectly. Print the counter and running total during the experiment. For menu choices, try a valid selection, a value outside the list, and a value of an unexpected kind. Decide which the instructions permit. Different BASIC dialects handle input details differently, so identify the intended interpreter rather than assuming every machine will recover from a bad entry in the same way.

A branch can be tested without building a whole game around it. If a cabinet requires a key, list the two states and the expected message for each. Test both before adding another object. Give variables names you can distinguish within the rules of your BASIC dialect; do not assume every interpreter treats long names in the same fashion. A program that appears to forget one fact may actually be reusing a variable in a way its author did not intend. The manual belongs beside the pencil, not on the distant shelf.

Finish the repair with a note describing the first wrong value, the cause, and the input that now checks the correction. Preserve that input as a future test. The note is useful when another change breaks the same behavior a month later. Debugging becomes less mysterious when it is a search for a disagreement between two explicit accounts: what should happen and what did happen. Even a beginner can conduct that search one variable and one line at a time, without pretending to understand every corner of a large program at once.

articles.title: The club budget that changes when one cell changes
articles.author: LotusLeaf
paragraphs: A spreadsheet earns its keep when it answers a question you expect to ask again. Our fictional club wants to know how many members must attend a workshop to cover the room and handout costs. Begin with the question on paper, then separate fixed costs, costs per attendee, and the amount collected per attendee. A worksheet that simply reproduces a printed total misses the interesting part. The goal is to change an assumption and see the consequences without retyping the whole calculation or losing track of which number was assumed.
